<comment datatype="string"><b>General Background</b>
<p>
<a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=METHYL-GLYOXAL">Methylglyoxal</a> is produced in small amounts during glycolysis
(via <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=DIHYDROXY-ACETONE-PHOSPHATE">glycerone phosphate</a>), fatty acid metabolism (via <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=ACETONE">acetone</a>),
and protein metabolism (via <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=AMINO-ACETONE">aminoacetone</a>). <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=METHYL-GLYOXAL">Methylglyoxal</a> is
highly toxic, most likely as a result of its interaction with protein side chains (see [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10597025">Kalapos99</a>] for
a review).
There are several pathways for the detoxification of methylglyoxal, based on different enzymes
that are able to convert methylglyoxal to less toxic compounds. These enzymes include glyoxalase
enzymes, methylglyoxal reductases, aldose reductases, aldehyde reductases and methylglyoxal
dehydrogenases.
<p>
<b>About This Pathway</b>
<p>
The glyoxalase system is probably the most common pathway that catalyzes the conversion of
methylglyoxal to a less toxic product. 
In this pathway, <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=METHYL-GLYOXAL">methylglyoxal</a> is converted to <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=D-LACTATE">(<i>R</i>)-lactate</a> via the intermediate
<a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=S-LACTOYL-GLUTATHIONE">(<i>R</i>)-<i>S</i>-lactoylglutathione</a> by 2 enzymes:
<p>
<a href="/gene?orgid=META&id=GLYOXI-MONOMER">glyoxalase I</a> isomerizes the hemithioacetal that is formed non-enzymatically from
<a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=METHYL-GLYOXAL">methylglyoxal</a> and <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=GLUTATHIONE">glutathione</a> to <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=S-LACTOYL-GLUTATHIONE">(<i>R</i>)-<i>S</i>-lactoylglutathione</a>.
<a href="/gene?orgid=META&id=GLYOXII-MONOMER">hydroxyacylglutathione hydrolase GloB</a> hydrolyzes the thioester to <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=D-LACTATE">(<i>R</i>)-lactate</a> regenerating the
glutathione in the process.
<p>
The fate of <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=D-LACTATE">(<i>R</i>)-lactate</a> has been less well characterized. The most likely scenario
is its conversion to <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=PYRUVATE">pyruvate</a> by the action of <a href="/gene?orgid=META&id=DLACTDEHYDROGFAD-MONOMER">D-lactate dehydrogenase</a>,
a flavoprotein specific to the D-form of lactate [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/497162">Olson79</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12127981">Flick02</a>].
<p>
The pathway is ubiquitous in biological life, taking place in the cytosol of prokaryotes and the
mitochondria of eukaryotes [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15987839">Ewaschuk05</a>].
<p>
</comment>

<comment datatype="string">Glyoxalase I catalyzes the first of two sequential steps in the conversion of methylgloxal to D-lactate.  The enzyme tightly binds one ion of nickel per enzyme dimer and is the first example of a nickel-containing glyoxalase [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9628737">Clugston98</a>].  Glyoxalase I shows lower levels of activity with a number of other metal ion cofactors including Co<sup>2+</sup>, but not including Zn<sup>2+</sup> [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/14556652">Clugston04</a>].
<p>
Crystal structures of glyoxalase I in the apo form and in complex with various metal ions have been determined [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10913283">He00</a>].  The nickel active site structure has been probed by X-ray absorption studies [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11196887">Davidson00</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11294624">Davidson01</a>].  The two active sites of the homodimer are initially asymmetric; only one site binds Ni<sup>2+</sup> [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/19053281">Su08</a>].
<p>
A <i>gloA</i> null mutant shows normal growth and viability, but sensitizes cells to both exogenously added and endogenously produced methylglyoxal, while a strain overexpressing <i>gloA</i> shows enhanced tolerance to methylglyoxal [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9489668">MacLean98</a>] and glyoxal [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/23506073">Lee13a</a>].  In a <i>gloA</i> mutant, higher levels of carnosine are required to protect the cells against methylglyoxal toxicity [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20952637">Pepper10</a>].  <i>gloA</i> appears to be co-transcribed with <i>nemRA</i> [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/23506073">Lee13a</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/23646895">Ozyamak13</a>]; its expression is induced in response to growth-inhibitory concentrations of methylglyoxal [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/23646895">Ozyamak13</a>]
<p>
Reviews: [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/21310258">Suttisansanee11</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18533363">Sukdeo08</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10226043">Maroney99</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2198020">Thornalley90</a>]</comment>

<comment datatype="string">D-lactate dehydrogenase (Dld) is a FAD-dependent peripheral membrane dehydrogenase catalysing the oxidation of D-lactate to pyruvate. Dld is a respiratory enzyme; electrons derived from D-lactate oxidation are transferred to the membrane soluble quinone pool [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/4582730">Kohn73</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/4575624">Futai73</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/3013300">Matsushita86</a>]. 
<p>
D-lactate dehydrogenase functions as a primary dehydrogenase in aerobic and anaerobic respiratory chains <i>invitro</i>. Electron transfer from D-lactate to oxygen under aerobic conditions and electron transfer from D-lactate to nitrate under anaerobic conditions depends on the presence of a quinone [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/195602">Wallace77</a>]. Anaerobic &beta;-galactoside transport in whole cells and membrane vesicles can be coupled to the oxidation of D-lactate with fumarate as a terminal acceptor [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/4587250">Konings73</a>].   
<p>
Proteoliposomes reconstituted with purified cytochrome <i>bo</i> oxidase, ubiquinone-8 and D-lactate dehydrogenase generate an H<sup>+</sup> electrochemical gradient (negative inside) in the presence of D-lactate. Studies using strains with defined respiratory enzyme composition suggest that the electron flow from D-lactate dehydrogenase to ubiquinone is not electrogenic [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/3013300">Matsushita86</a>]. Membrane vesicles prepared from Dld negative mutants do not catalyse D-lactate oxidation [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/4343963">Hong72</a>].   
<p>
The crystal structure has been solved at 1.9 &Aring; resolution. The protein contains 3 discontinuous domains - a FAD binding domain, a cap domain and a membrane binding domain. The membrane domain of Dld has an electropositive surface; Dld binds to the membrane through electrostatic force [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10944213">Dym00</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2185834">Peersen90</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8268803">Sun93</a>]. 
<p>
D-lactate dehydrogenase was widely used in experiments investigating the mechanism for energy coupling between respiration and active transport (see articles by [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/4363926">Lombardi74</a>], [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/4275121">Harold74</a>] and [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/4620043">Kaback74</a>]).  
<p>
<i>E. coli</i> K-12 also contains a membrane bound <a href="/gene?orgid=META&id=L-LACTDEHYDROGFMN-MONOMER">L-lactate dehydrogenase</a> and a soluble NAD-linked fermentative  <a href="/gene?orgid=META&id=DLACTDEHYDROGNAD-MONOMER">D-lactate dehydrogenase</a>.
<p>
Review: [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2655708">Ho89</a>]</comment>

<comment datatype="string">Glyoxalase II catalyzes the second of two sequential reactions in the conversion of methylglyoxal to D-lactate [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2198020">Thornalley90</a>]. 
<p>
The enzyme contains ~1.7 molecules of Zn<sup>2+</sup> per active monomer.  Co<sup>2+</sup> and Mn<sup>2+</sup> can substitute for Zn<sup>2+</sup>, but Ni<sup>2+</sup> can not [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17196158">Oyoung07</a>].
<p>
A <i>gloB</i> null mutant accumulates S-lactoylglutathione upon methylglyoxal exposure and has a depleted glutathione pool.  This leads to activation of the KefB potassium efflux system, which causes cytoplasmic acidification and protection against methylglyoxal toxicity.  Conversely, overexpression of <i>gloB</i> leads to depletion of S-lactoylglutathione and increased sensitivity to methylglyoxal [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/21143325">Ozyamak10</a>].
<p>
<i>gloB</i> shows differential codon adaptation, resulting in differential translation efficiency signatures, in thermophilic microbes.  It was therefore predicted to play a role in the heat shock response.  A <i>gloB</i> deletion mutant was shown to be more sensitive than wild-type specifically to heat shock, but not other stresses [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24580753">Kri14</a>].  Single <i>gloB</i> and <a href="/gene?orgid=META&id=G6475"><i>gloC</i></a> mutants show decreased methylglyoxal tolerance; a &Delta;<i>gloBC</i> double deletion mutant is more sensitive to methylglyoxal than either single mutant [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25670698">Reiger15</a>].
<p>
Reviews: [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/21310258">Suttisansanee11</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18533363">Sukdeo08</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2198020">Thornalley90</a>]</comment>

texts.value: Catalyzes the isomerization of the hemithioacetal formed spontaneously from methylglyoxal and glutathione, to S-lactoylglutathione, which is then hydrolyzed by a type II glyoxalase (GloB or GloC). Is involved in methylglyoxal (MG) detoxification (Probable) (PubMed:10913283). Involved in resistance to hypochlorous acid (HOCl), which is the active component of household bleach and a powerful antimicrobial during the innate immune response (PubMed:23536188)
Binds 1 nickel ion per subunit. In the homodimer, two nickel ions are bound between subunits. Is not active with zinc ions.
Secondary metabolite metabolism; methylglyoxal degradation; (R)-lactate from methylglyoxal: step 1/2
Homodimer
Repressed by NemR. Induced by reactive electrophilic species (RES) such as quinones, glyoxals and methylglyoxal (PubMed:23506073, PubMed:23646895). Up-regulated by HOCl (PubMed:23536188)
Deletion of the gene increases the HOCl sensitivity. Mutant is more sensitive to methylglyoxal treatment
Belongs to the glyoxalase I family

Type II glyoxalase that catalyzes the hydrolysis of (R)-S-lactoylglutathione to (R)-lactate and glutathione (PubMed:17196158, PubMed:25670698). Is more efficient than the isozyme GloC, and plays a major contribution to methylglyoxal (MG) detoxification in E.coli (PubMed:25670698). The two isoenzymes have additive effects and ensure maximal MG degradation (PubMed:25670698)

reaction.name: an S-(2-hydroxyacyl)glutathione + H2O = a 2-hydroxy carboxylate + glutathione + H(+)

texts.value: Binds 2 Zn(2+) ions per subunit. Mn(2+) and Co(2+) can substitute for zinc in reconstitution experiments.
Is inhibited by Cu(2+)
kcat is 53 sec(-1) for the hydrolysis of (R)-S-lactoylglutathione (PubMed:17196158). kcat is 15.6 sec(-1) for the hydrolysis of (R)-S-lactoylglutathione (PubMed:25670698).
Secondary metabolite metabolism; methylglyoxal degradation; (R)-lactate from methylglyoxal: step 2/2
Monomer

Cells lacking this gene show decreased methylglyoxal tolerance. A double deletion mutant lacking both gloB and gloC exhibits almost no resistance to exogenously supplied methylglyoxal, and is unable to grow at MG concentrations as low as 0.1 mM
Belongs to the metallo-beta-lactamase superfamily. Glyoxalase II family

Catalyzes the oxidation of D-lactate to pyruvate. Electrons derived from D-lactate oxidation are transferred to the ubiquinone/cytochrome electron transfer chain, where they may be used to provide energy for the active transport of a variety of amino acids and sugars across the membrane
Inhibited by 2-hydroxy-3-butynoic acid, but not by p-chloromercuribenzoate, n-ethylmaleimide, or 5,5'-dithiobis(2-nitrobenzoic acid)
May bind the membrane through electrostatic rather than hydrophobic forces
Contains 3 domains: the flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD)-binding domain, the cap domain and the membrane-binding domain
Belongs to the quinone-dependent D-lactate dehydrogenase family

F:oxidoreductase activity, acting on the CH-OH group of donors, quinone or similar compound as acceptor

native_dispositions.disposition: Retain whole GloA step with independently verified MetaCyc assembly and Rhea19071. Preserve two-chain native coefficient. Net reaction includes spontaneous hemithioacetal formation, not direct enzyme-catalyzed condensation.
Retain GloB-specific hydrolysis as Rhea25246 with correct R-lactate. Accessory GloC supported by current primary annotation, outside the exact native GloB controller projection; no exclusivity claim.
Retain Dld oxidation to pyruvate, independently Rhea51469. No native Rhea exactMatch asserted.

Native label L-lactic acid, BioCyc L-LACTATE and CHEBI422 identify S-acid; supplied SMILES C[C@@H](O)C(O)=O has opposite stereo from authority CHEBI422 C[C@H](O)C(=O)O. Reject inconsistent native identity and independently ground D-(R)-lactate CHEBI16004 from Rhea, UniProt and primary. No stereo-preserving native exactMatch asserted.
Native formula, SMILES, CHEBI16856 identify reduced glutathione; BioCyc OXIDIZED-GLUTATHIONE xref contradicts them and is rejected. Select Rhea charge form CHEBI57925, not glutathione disulfide.
Native R-S-lactoylglutathione neutral form CHEBI15694 is compatible with stereochemistry; select independently verified deprotonated Rhea species CHEBI57474.

Native UQ6/UQ6H2 are real chemical identities but unsubstantiated chain-length specificity for this E. coli reaction. Use independently curated quinone/quinol classes CHEBI132124/CHEBI24646. PMID3013300 supports UQ8 reconstitution, not UQ6; do not assert exact equivalence of specific and generic entities.
Native neutral pyruvic acid replaced by independently verified Rhea pyruvate CHEBI15361; protonation change explicit, not exact identity.
Methylglyoxal, water and hydron identities retained with independent Rhea/ChEBI grounding.

Native species E. coli562; named proteins K-12 83333. MetaCyc includes MG1655511145; primary2022 SIJ488 derivatives are engineered MG1655 descendants. RecordK12 scope does not claim everystrain/condition flux.
